View image in fullscreen 
A painting depicting Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping is unveiled in St Petersburg, Russia. Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP 
Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
Russia and US approach potential summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice, as Putin hopes to find consensus on new global order 
T he Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is among those who have expressed concern that the world will witness a Yalta 2.0 moment if Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet trilaterally, as expected, on the sidelines of the Apec summit in China next week. 
It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. 
Putin has long proposed this re-enactment of the greatest wartime summit, held in February 1945 at Joseph Stalin’s insistence in a rundown Tsarist resort on the south coast of Crimea alongside Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill. 
Trump has cast himself in the role of the enthusiastic guest while Xi acts the bashful host, ever reluctant to embrace the status of a traditional global superpower. 
No one quite knows what will happen if the three men meet or even if China will allow more than a stiff protocol-driven exchange of statements. China is already trying to push nuclear disarmament off the agenda. 
It may prove to be little more than abbreviated geopolitical theatre that Putin can retail domestically to show that Russia – even with an economy seven times smaller than that of the EU – still plays with the big boys. 
View image in fullscreen 
The three world leaders are expected to hold a meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzen. Photograph: Yin Haixiang/VCG/Getty Images 
But if Putin has his way he will try to ensure that this becomes the first of a series of meetings in this format in which the big powers organise a new world order on a set of security oriented principles in which liberal values play little part. 
As Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, told Russian TV: “The task is to create a comprehensive system of comprehensive security in Europe that will become a new modern Yalta or Potsdam. If we manage to create such a security system then we will ensure peace in Europe for decades, perhaps even centuries. That is our main task.” 
Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, said the summit could mark “the start of a return from this slide into absolute chaos to stabilisation”. For Zelenskyy, the concern is that almost any time Putin and Trump converse, it is Kyiv that suffers. 
The original Yalta is widely remembered, outside Russia, as a moment of cynical trade-offs, even ignominy, to rival the appeasement of the 1938 Munich agreement. It was eight days that shaped the postwar world in which absent countries were discarded or divided by the imminent wartime victors. 
FDR, months from death, was intent on enlisting Russian support for a new League of Nations organisation and for Russian participation in the war against Japan. In return, he accepted the fait accompli of Russia’s presence in Poland, and covered his treacherous tracks by persuading Stalin to sign a declaration that affirmed the principles of “sovereign rights and self-government” should prevail in countries freed from Nazi rule. 
Few thought the dictator had any intent to honour the agreement. Indeed, honour was somewhat absent throughout the eight days. When Churchill told Stalin it was a “matter of honour” that the independence of Poland, Britain’s original casus belli , was preserved, Stalin replied the issue for him was “a matter of life and death”. Churchill had no means to confront Stalin since by then he was the victor of Stalingrad and Kursk, and the commander of an army that had crushed Germany. 
View image in fullscreen 
Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin at the Yalta summit in 1945, where the postwar world was shaped. Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images 
The subsequent sense of shame about the betrayal of Yalta accumulated mostly in America, so much so that in May 2005, before a trip to Moscow for the 60th anniversary of Victory in Europe Day, George Bush told an audience in Latvia that Yalta had “consigned millions to communist captivity. When powerful nations negotiated, the freedom of small nations was somehow expendable. Yet this attempt to sacrifice freedom for the sake of stability left a continent divided and unstable.” It was a view shared across Europe. 
The Republican tradition expressed by Bush has been expunged by Trump. In his 2025 national security document, Trump lauded the sphere of influence geopolitics championed at Yalta. He named the western hemisphere as America’s domain. It remained deferential to Russia and China’s spheres. 
Unfortunately, Trump took little notice of the strategy prepared for him. He retained his respect for Putin and Xi, but indulged himself, and Israel, in a disastrous imperial overreach elsewhere, notably in Iran . skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
As a result, the US and Russia are approaching the summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice that have wounded them. Xi is cast in the role of Stalin, hosting two countries in need of his beneficence. 
It leaves China somewhat wary, reluctant to use its leverage if it helps the US, or is seen to run counter to the Chinese narrative of being a force for stability and coexistence. Speaking at the Emirates Policy Center conference in Abu Dhabi, Prof Minghao Zhao from Fudan University gave a classic exposition of Chinese non-interference. “The Russia-Ukraine war is the strategic mistake made by the Russian president. The Iran war is the strategic mistake made by President Trump. China is managing the consequences of those conflicts.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Trump, Putin and Xi as matryoshkas, the traditional Russian wooden dolls. Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP 
By contrast, Dr Wang Huiyao, the president of the Center for China and Globalization and an early advocate of a trilateral summit, argued China was needed. He referenced the Kindleberger trap – a period of chaos caused by too little global leadership. He said China was trying to be helpful by propping up multilateralism and might provide guarantees in Iran, something the Iranian leadership favours, but even he saw China’s stabilisation role largely through the prism of developing the global economy. 
In short, China might help extricate Trump in the Middle East. After all, open waterways are necessary to meet its insatiable demand for oil. 
But China sees Ukraine as a strictly European security issue in which it is not willing to betray Putin, or endorse a settlement reached without Europe’s agreement. China is in the midst of repairing relations with Europe after China’s industrial overcapacity in 2025 flooded the European market, risking its deindustrialisation. China’s embrace of Putin’s vision of a new European security architecture would infuriate Germany and the European Commission. 
For some, such as John Ikenberry, the theorist of liberal internationalism, the sight of the US president carving up the world with autocrats is anathema. He thinks there is a viable alliance of democracies. 
But Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, says more Yaltas are the future. “We have to learn to work across the geopolitical and ideological dividing lines,” he said. “We are now in a world in which the US and its democratic allies are no longer the preponderant coalition. 
“Who is coming up? China, India, Indonesia, large countries of the global south – all of then playing the field and most of them have closer economic ties with China than with the US. 
“We are going to have to learn to work with autocracies and to live with them more comfortably. Is there a downside risk? Sure. Might Trump throw Taiwan and Ukraine under the bus? Possibly, but I doubt it. But we need to break the ice. These conversations have to start now and I give credit to President Trump for starting it.”

articles.full_text:
Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick shake hands at the G20 innovation ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on 2 September. Photograph: Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty Images 
View image in fullscreen 
Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick shake hands at the G20 innovation ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on 2 September. Photograph: Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty Images 
Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action
US commerce secretary faces sack as questions emerge over senior Trump officials’ knowledge of alleged Chinese spy’s ties to Jensen Huang 
- 
US politics – live updates 
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, is facing growing pressure over his apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal as other Trump administration officials publicly raise questions over his decisions. 
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China. 
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by the company’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress , after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. 
White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported, after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration . 
Lutnick is now scheduled to testify before Congress next month, just days after the ousted Nvidia chief answers lawmakers’ questions on Capitol Hill. 
Lutnick is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration. 
Bessent has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added in an interview with the network on Friday. 
View image in fullscreen 
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, on 22 May 2025. Photograph: CTI/AFPTV/AFP/Getty Images 
John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”. 
The Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times that there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls”, adding: “Heads should roll.” A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang 
Read more 
The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether US security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang. 
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News. 
Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge . The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported . 
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Photograph: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images 
The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia. 
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair, said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him, citing “recent reports [that] raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology”. Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached? 
Read more 
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal-conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to his “profound” contributions to the company he cofounded. 
Huang is reported to have had relationships with Alice Huang as well as an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times, and another, unnamed employee, according to Reuters. 
The House foreign affairs chair, Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony. 
View image in fullscreen 
The Taiwan Stock Exchange opened 627.88 points higher on Friday, at 43,719.75, with a turnover of 21.86bn New Taiwan dollars ($662.87m), amid uncertainty in the AI sector. Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPA 
The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China . 
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company important to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them. 
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding that he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“ 
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters . 
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models. 
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday. 
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as Huang’s swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for more than three decades. 
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo. 
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
